question.problem:
Consider the function $y=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}.$ The derivative of this function is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}-1}}{{e}^{2-4x}}((x+2)^{2}+g(x)).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$
question.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}.
$$

First, we find the natural logarithm of both sides and use the quotient and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((x+1)^{{x}^{2}})-\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{2-4x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-(2-4x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-2+4x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{x+1}+4 \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x+1}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x+1}+4)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{x+1}+4) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(\frac{2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}+4(x+1)}{x+1}) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}-1}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}+4(x+1)) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}-1}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+{x}^{2}+4x+4) \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{{x}^{2}-1}}{{e}^{2-4x}}(2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+(x+2)^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x)=2x(x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1).
$$
